screens.title: Resilience Patterns and Chaos Engineering
screens.subtitle: Design software to survive failures and verify it with controlled experiments

narration.text: In this chapter you will learn how to design applications that continue to operate when dependencies fail, and how to validate those designs by intentionally injecting faults. We start with three practical resilience patterns — circuit breaker, bulkhead, and retry with exponential backoff — each of which protects different resources and failure modes. Then we'll introduce Chaos Engineering as a discipline: how to form hypotheses about behavior under failure, run controlled experiments, and automate them. Finally, you'll see how AWS Fault Injection Simulator helps run safe experiments by targeting resources, performing actions like terminating instances or injecting latency, and enforcing stop conditions tied to CloudWatch metrics. This knowledge matters because infrastructure redundancy alone can't prevent application-level cascades or resource exhaustion. By combining resilient design with continuous, automated testing, you gain confidence that your system will recover gracefully. As you move through the lesson, think of a recent outage or slowdown you observed and which pattern might have reduced its impact.

keyIdea.title: Why this chapter matters
keyIdea.text: Resilience patterns limit failure blast radius; Chaos Engineering tests those patterns in safe, controlled ways so you can find and fix weaknesses before customers notice.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you'll be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: By the end of this chapter you will be able to identify and apply common resilience patterns, explain the core principles of Chaos Engineering, and design controlled experiments using AWS Fault Injection Simulator. First, you will recognize when to use a circuit breaker to prevent cascading failures and be able to describe the half-open, open, and closed states. Second, you'll understand bulkheads and how resource isolation prevents one failing dependency from exhausting system resources. Third, you will apply retry patterns with exponential backoff and jitter to treat transient failures without overwhelming a recovering service. Fourth, you'll define an FIS experiment: selecting targets, specifying actions, and crafting stop conditions tied to CloudWatch metrics. Each objective connects to operational practices: for example, writing a hypothesis for an FIS test forces you to state expected behavior and measurable metrics. These skills matter because implementing patterns without verification leaves gaps; testing with FIS and stop conditions gives you the evidence to improve monitoring, alerts, and runbooks. As you learn each objective, consider a system you operate and which objective would most improve its reliability first.

screens.title: Circuit Breaker Pattern
screens.subtitle: Detect and fail fast to protect the system

narration.text: A circuit breaker is a guard that prevents an unhealthy dependency from dragging down the calling system. Conceptually it tracks recent call failures or timeouts to an external service and transitions between three states: closed (normal calls pass), open (calls fail fast), and half-open (a small number of test calls are allowed). The key benefit is that failing fast conserves threads, connection pools, and downstream capacity so the rest of the application can continue. For example, if a payment A P I starts timing out, the circuit breaker opens after repeated failures so the checkout flow can respond quickly with a fallback or a user-friendly error instead of blocking threads. A common configuration is to set sliding-window thresholds, a cooldown timeout, and a conservative half-open probe size. A common misconception is that circuit breakers hide problems; they do not fix the remote service but they prevent cascading resource exhaustion and buy time for recovery. When you implement a breaker, instrument the state changes and include clear alerts for 'open' events. Takeaway: use circuit breakers to fail fast, protect shared resources, and provide observability so engineers know when an external service is struggling.

keyIdea.title: Protect shared resources
keyIdea.text: Circuit breakers fail fast to prevent one bad dependency from consuming all resources.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.6 › Circuit Breaker
Definition

A mechanism that monitors calls to an external dependency and stops attempting calls when the dependency is unhealthy to prevent cascading failures.

States
  • Closed: calls pass normally.
  • Open: calls fail immediately to conserve resources.
  • Half-open: test calls to probe recovery.
Configuration knobs
Sliding window failure threshold, timeout, cooldown period, and probe size for half-open checks.
Example
If payment API times out repeatedly, open the breaker so checkout returns a friendly message and retries later.
Illustration & Explanation
Failure Flow
Repeated failures → open breaker → fast failure responses → recovery probe.
Monitoring
Emit events when state changes and alert on sustained open state so engineers can investigate.
Key Takeaway

Circuit breakers reduce blast radius and conserve resources; always pair them with observability and alerts.

screens.title: Bulkhead Pattern
screens.subtitle: Isolate components so one failure doesn't sink the whole system

narration.text: The bulkhead pattern isolates resources so failure in one component does not consume all shared capacity. Think of a ship's compartments: a breach in one section doesn't sink the vessel if the others remain sealed. In software terms, this means dedicating threads, connection pools, or worker queues to individual dependencies so a slow dependency cannot starve the rest of the system. For example, if a reporting service uses a small worker pool separate from the transaction processing pool, a backlog in reporting won't delay payment processing. Implementing bulkheads can be done at multiple levels: per-thread pool, per-service container, or per-request semaphore. A common mistake is over-isolation, which reduces overall utilization; balance is required between fault isolation and efficient resource use. Monitoring should track queue lengths and saturation per bulkhead to detect pressure before failures occur. Takeaway: use bulkheads to contain resource consumption and preserve critical paths, and tune sizes based on realistic load testing. Bulkhead Pattern means bulkheads reserve capacity so a faulty component cannot starve critical operations.. In practical terms, isolate components so one failure doesn't sink the whole system. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Contain resource consumption
keyIdea.text: Bulkheads reserve capacity so a faulty component cannot starve critical operations.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.6 › Bulkhead Pattern
Definition & analogy

Bulkhead isolates failures by partitioning resources so one component's failure cannot consume all capacity and affect others.

Where to apply
Microservices calling external APIs, background workers, and shared thread pools are common places.
Implementation options
  • Separate thread pools or semaphores per external call.
  • Per-service container limits and resource requests.
  • Dedicated queues for non-critical processing.
Example

If a third-party analytics API becomes slow, limit concurrency for analytics calls to keep checkout and login flows responsive. This keeps critical user journeys operating while the analytics backlog grows in a controlled way.

Monitoring
Track saturation and queue length per partition to trigger scaling or throttling before failures escalate.
Misconception
Isolation isn't free: overly small partitions reduce throughput; find the right balance with load tests.
Key Takeaway

Partition resources to protect critical paths; tune bulkheads based on realistic load and monitoring.

screens.title: Retry Pattern with Exponential Backoff and Jitter
screens.subtitle: Recover from transient faults without creating thundering herds

narration.text: Retries are a simple way to handle transient failures, but naive retries can worsen outages by overloading a recovering service. The recommended approach is exponential backoff: increase the wait time between attempts exponentially so the service has time to recover. Adding jitter—small randomization to each delay—prevents synchronized retries from forming a thundering herd. For example, after a network hiccup, retry the A P I call after 100 milliseconds, then 200, then 400, with a small random variation on each delay. Many AWS SDKs use exponential backoff with jitter by default for A P I retries. Important configuration choices include maximum attempts, base delay, maximum delay cap, and whether to retry on specific status codes or exceptions only. A common misconception is to retry forever or to use very short delays; both can amplify failure. Pair retries with circuit breakers: if retries continue to fail and consume resources, the circuit breaker should open to stop futile retries. Takeaway: design retries conservatively, prefer exponential backoff with jitter, and combine with observability and breakers. Retry Pattern with Exponential Backoff and Jitter means use exponential backoff with jitter and combine retries with circuit breakers to avoid amplifying failures.. In practical terms, recover from transient faults without creating thundering herds. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Retry intelligently
keyIdea.text: Use exponential backoff with jitter and combine retries with circuit breakers to avoid amplifying failures.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.6 › Retry + Backoff
Pattern

Retry the operation on transient errors, increasing delay between attempts exponentially. Add jitter to avoid synchronized retries across clients.

Parameters
  • Base delay, multiplier, max delay cap.
  • Maximum attempts and retryable error list.
  • Jitter strategy: randomize each delay slightly.
Integration
Combine retries with circuit breakers and bulkheads to protect resources while recovering from transient faults.
Concrete example
After a network timeout, retry with delays of 100ms, 200ms, 400ms, each with ±20ms random jitter, and stop after 4 attempts. If failures continue, the circuit breaker should open to prevent further retries.
Misconception
Retrying immediately or indefinitely will likely worsen an outage rather than fix it.
Key Takeaway

Retries are useful for transient faults but must back off and include randomness; combine with breakers for safety.

screens.title: When to Use Each Pattern
screens.subtitle: Match failure mode to the right protection

narration.text: Choosing among circuit breaker, bulkhead, and retry requires mapping the failure mode to the protection each pattern provides. Use circuit breakers when a remote service becomes consistently error-prone or slow; the breaker prevents repeated attempts and conserves resources. Use bulkheads when a component's resource usage, such as threads or connections, can starve other parts of the system—this isolates the impact. Use retry with exponential backoff and jitter for transient, short-lived errors like momentary network glitches. A concrete scenario: if an external payment provider intermittently returns timeouts, first implement retries with backoff and jitter for brief hiccups. If timeouts persist and saturate threads, add a circuit breaker to fail fast. If reporting or analytics calls cause high connection usage, put them into a separate bulkhead so critical transaction paths remain available. A typical misconception is to stack retries and ignore circuit breakers; this can lead to resource exhaustion. The correct approach combines patterns selectively and observes real traffic to tune parameters. When to Use Each Pattern means use retries for transient faults, circuit breakers for persistent failures, and bulkheads to isolate resource consumption.. In practical terms, match failure mode to the right protection. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Choose patterns by failure mode
keyIdea.text: Use retries for transient faults, circuit breakers for persistent failures, and bulkheads to isolate resource consumption.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.6 › Pattern Comparison
Retry
Use for transient errors
Short-lived network glitches or momentary service hiccups. Use exponential backoff and jitter.
Circuit Breaker
Use for persistent failures
When a dependency is repeatedly failing or timing out, fail fast to conserve resources and probe recovery later.
Bulkhead
Use for resource isolation
Prevent resource exhaustion by partitioning threads, queues, or containers for non-critical workloads.
Practical scenario
If a payment API intermittently times out, start with retries and backoff. If timeouts persist, introduce a circuit breaker. If analytics calls consume threads, add bulkheads to preserve the payment path.

screens.title: Chaos Engineering Principles
screens.subtitle: Experiment to build confidence in resilience

narration.text: Chaos Engineering is the discipline of running experiments on a system to gain confidence in its ability to withstand real-world turbulence. The approach begins with a hypothesis about expected behavior under a defined failure. You then introduce controlled variability—such as terminating instances, adding network latency, or throttling APIs—and observe whether the system meets the hypothesis. Experiments should start small, run in production-like environments when safe, and be automated to provide continuous coverage. Key principles include formulating a clear hypothesis, varying a real-world event, running experiments where they matter, and automating them. An example hypothesis might be: if 25% of ASG instances are terminated, the ALB 5XX rate remains below one percent and the ASG replaces instances within five minutes. A common misconception is that chaos is reckless destruction; performed correctly, experiments are tightly scoped, monitored, and include automated stop conditions to prevent harm. Takeaway: Chaos Engineering reveals assumptions and weak points so you can turn them into measurable improvements. Chaos Engineering Principles means chaos engineering uses hypothesis-driven, measurable experiments to find weaknesses before they affect customers.. In practical terms, experiment to build confidence in resilience. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Core steps
  1. Formulate a hypothesis about system behavior under a fault.
  2. Introduce a real-world event such as instance termination or latency.
  3. Observe, measure, and compare results to the hypothesis.
  4. Fix issues and iterate, automating experiments when useful.
Safety practices

  • Define stop conditions and ensure monitoring covers them.
  • Inform on-call staff and validate runbooks before experiments.
Key Takeaway

Chaos is a tool for learning. Use hypothesis-driven, measured experiments to make systems measurably more resilient.

screens.title: AWS Fault Injection Simulator (FIS)
screens.subtitle: A managed service for running chaos experiments on AWS

narration.text: AWS Fault Injection Simulator provides a managed way to run chaos experiments in AWS by declaring templates that specify targets, actions, and stop conditions. With FIS you select targets—such as specific EC2 instances or an auto scaling group—choose actions like instance termination or network latency injection, and configure parameters and IAM permissions the service needs. Stop conditions, typically tied to CloudWatch metrics, ensure the experiment halts automatically if metrics indicate unacceptable impact. For example, you can stop an experiment if the ALB 5XX count exceeds a defined threshold. FIS integrates with tags and ARNs to precisely scope experiments and supports templating so tests are repeatable and automatable. A common pitfall is insufficiently narrow targets or missing stop conditions; always scope experiments to the smallest viable blast radius and test stop logic ahead of time. Takeaway: FIS reduces operational lift for chaos experiments by managing execution and providing guardrails through stop conditions and IAM roles. AWS Fault Injection Simulator (FIS) means fis lets you declare repeatable experiments with actions, targets, and stop conditions so you can safely test resilience on aws.. In practical terms, a managed service for running chaos experiments on aws. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Managed fault injection
keyIdea.text: FIS lets you declare repeatable experiments with actions, targets, and stop conditions so you can safely test resilience on AWS.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.6 › AWS FIS
Elements of an FIS template
  • Targets: which resources will be affected (instances, ASGs).
  • Actions: what fault to inject (terminate, latency).
  • Stop conditions: CloudWatch metrics that halt the experiment.
  • IAM role: permissions FIS needs to perform actions and read metrics.
Safety note

Always start with small, reversible experiments and test stop conditions in staging. Use tags or ARNs to target specific instances and avoid broad-scoped experiments that could impact production users unnecessarily.

Conceptual CLI snippet
# Conceptual FIS experiment template (simplified)
aws fis create-experiment-template \
  --description "Terminate random EC2 instances in an ASG" \
  --tags '{"Project":"MyWebApp"}' \
  --actions '{
    "TerminateInstances": {
      "ActionId": "aws:ec2:terminate-instances",
      "Parameters": { "instanceTerminationPercentage": "50" },
      "Targets": { "Instances": "MyWebAppASGInstances" }
    }
  }' \
  --targets '{
    "MyWebAppASGInstances": {
      "ResourceType": "aws:ec2:instance",
      "SelectionMode": "COUNT(2)",
      "Parameters": { "filters": [{"path":"State.Name","values":["running"]}], "resourceArns": ["arn:aws:ec2:us-east-1:123456789012:auto-scaling-group/MyWebAppASG"] }
    }
  }' \
  --stop-conditions '[{"Source":"cloudwatch","Value":"ALB_HTTP_5XX_COUNT","Threshold":"100","ComparisonOperator":"GREATER_THAN_OR_EQUAL"}]' \
  --role-arn "arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/FISRole"

screens.title: Designing a Safe FIS Experiment
screens.subtitle: Hypothesis, targets, actions, stop conditions, and review

narration.text: Designing a safe experiment begins with a clear hypothesis that states expected behavior and measurable metrics. For instance: if 25% of ASG instances are terminated, ALB 5XX errors remain below one percent and the ASG replaces instances within five minutes. Next, choose narrow targets—specific ASG ARNs or tagged instances—and actions such as terminating a percentage of instances. Then define stop conditions tied to CloudWatch metrics that immediately halt the experiment if thresholds are breached, for example an increase in 5XX responses or C P U saturation above a set point. Ensure the experiment role has minimal permissions needed to perform actions and read metrics. Before running, validate monitoring and alerting, inform on-call staff, and ensure runbooks are prepared. After the experiment, review results against the hypothesis: did the system meet expectations, did alerts trigger correctly, and what configuration or code changes are required? A common mistake is skipping the hypothesis or stop conditions; without them, experiments can produce ambiguous outcomes or unnecessary harm. Takeaway: craft a narrow, measurable experiment with built-in safety and a clear remediation path. Designing a Safe FIS Experiment means a safe fis run includes a hypothesis, small targets, explicit stop conditions, and post-run remediation steps.. In practical terms, hypothesis, targets, actions, stop conditions, and review. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Experiment lifecycle
keyIdea.text: A safe FIS run includes a hypothesis, small targets, explicit stop conditions, and post-run remediation steps.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.6 › Design an FIS Experiment
Step-by-step
1. Hypothesis: Define expected behavior and measurable metrics.
2. Target: Narrow scope by ASG ARN or tags to reduce blast radius.
3. Action: Choose fault type and parameters (terminate, latency, throttle).
4. Stop Conditions: CloudWatch thresholds that halt the experiment automatically.
5. Review: Validate monitoring and runbooks, inform operations, then run and inspect results.
Concrete scenario

Hypothesis: Terminating 25% of ASG instances keeps ALB 5XX below 1%. Target: ASG ARN. Action: terminate count=25%. Stop condition: ALB 5XX >= 10 for 1 minute. Review alerts, logs, and recovery time after the run.

Pitfall
Skipping stop conditions or not notifying on-call teams increases the risk of unintended customer impact.
Key Takeaway

Design narrow, measurable experiments with clear stop conditions and a remediation plan.

screens.title: Hands-on Activity: ASG Self-Healing Test (Conceptual)
screens.subtitle: Design the hypothesis and the FIS template conceptually

narration.text: This activity walks through a conceptual design for testing an Auto Scaling Group's self-healing behavior. Start by writing a hypothesis: if 25% of EC2 instances in an ASG are terminated, the ALB's 5XX count will remain below an acceptable threshold and the ASG will replace instances within five minutes. Next define the target as the ASG's ARN or instances tagged for the test, and choose an action such as the EC2 terminate-instances action with parameters specifying percentage or count. Define stop conditions using CloudWatch metrics, for example ALB HTTP 5XX count greater than a threshold for a short evaluation period. Finally, ensure the FIS role has the minimal permissions needed to terminate instances and read metrics. A common misconception is that running the template once is sufficient; instead, iterate and automate tests so you measure improvements over time. After the experiment, compare metrics against your hypothesis, update runbooks if behavior deviates, and adjust bulkheads or breaker thresholds accordingly. Takeaway: a clear hypothesis and stop conditions are the most important parts of a safe, useful experiment. keyIdea.text: A clear hypothesis and targeted scope make FIS experiments safe and actionable; iterate to improve confidence.

Module 7 › Chapter 7.6 › Hands-on Activity
Hypothesis template
Example hypothesis to use: If 25% of instances in the ASG are terminated, ALB 5XX rate will remain below 1% and ASG will replace terminated instances within five minutes.
Target: ASG ARN or instance tag selector.

Post-run review

  2. Confirm alerts and runbook actions executed as expected.
  3. Update circuit breaker thresholds, bulkhead sizes, or scaling policies as needed.
Key Takeaway

Design experiments to produce clear yes/no answers against your hypothesis to enable focused remediation.

narration.text: There are several recurring mistakes when teams adopt resilience patterns or run chaos experiments. First, assuming patterns are effective without testing leaves blind spots; putting a circuit breaker in place doesn't guarantee correct thresholds or observability. Second, running experiments without stop conditions or adequate monitoring risks causing customer impact. Third, overly aggressive retries or improperly sized bulkheads can either amplify failure or underutilize capacity. To avoid these pitfalls, instrument pattern behavior: emit events when a circuit opens, measure bulkhead saturation, and track retry counts and latencies. Always define and test stop conditions and run experiments first in staging environments. Also practice incident response by reviewing the experiment's alerts and the runbook before widening scope. A practical safety step is to use small selection modes in FIS such as COUNT(1) or PERCENT(5) and short durations, then increase scope only when confidence grows. Takeaway: combine patterns, verify them with measured experiments, and enforce safety rules so resilience becomes demonstrable, not assumed. Common Mistakes and Safety Practices means implement patterns, then verify them with controlled experiments and robust monitoring to avoid false confidence.. In practical terms, avoiding overconfidence and accidental outages. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Don't assume resilience
keyIdea.text: Implement patterns, then verify them with controlled experiments and robust monitoring to avoid false confidence.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.6 › Mistakes & Safety
Top mistakes
  • Assuming patterns are effective without testing them.
  • Running experiments with no stop conditions or poor monitoring.
  • Retrying too aggressively and creating a thundering herd.
  • Over-isolating with bulkheads and reducing utilization unnecessarily.
Safety checklist
Validate stop conditions and ensure CloudWatch metrics are available to FIS.
Inform on-call teams and confirm runbooks are ready.
Scope experiments narrowly and iterate from staging to production.
Key Takeaway

Safety and observability are as important as the experiment itself; design tests to fail safely and yield clear, actionable results.

screens.title: From Patterns to Practice
screens.subtitle: Integrating resilience into operations and development

narration.text: Turning resilience patterns and chaos experiments into operational practice requires collaboration between SysOps and developers. Start by instrumenting patterns so their behavior is visible: log circuit breaker state transitions, surface retry counts and latencies, and expose bulkhead saturation metrics. Next, bake resilience into deployment pipelines by running automated experiments or simulations as part of pre-deploy checks in production-like environments. Use FIS templates as versioned artifacts that the team can reuse and refine. After experiments, perform a blameless review: did monitoring alert appropriately, did the runbook steps execute, and what configuration or code changes are needed to improve outcomes? A common misconception is that resilience is a one-time project; instead, treat it as continuous improvement. Finally, prioritize fixes based on customer impact and remediation effort—start with changes that close critical gaps and automate tests to prevent regressions. Takeaway: instrument, automate, and iterate so resilience becomes part of your delivery lifecycle. From Patterns to Practice means instrument pattern behavior, automate tests, and conduct post-experiment reviews to continuously improve system resilience.. In practical terms, integrating resilience into operations and development. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Part 1
screens.subtitle: What to remember from this chapter

narration.text: These are the most important ideas to carry forward. First: resilience patterns are not mutually exclusive; choose the pattern that addresses the failure mode and combine them as needed. Second: circuit breakers fail fast to prevent cascades; instrument their state transitions and configure sensible timeouts. Third: bulkheads partition resources to prevent one component from exhausting shared capacity. Keep these concepts front of mind when designing or operating services so you protect core user journeys under stress. As you apply these ideas, remember to pair technical controls with observability so you can measure their effectiveness. A short exercise: pick a service you operate, identify its most critical dependency, and ask which one of these three patterns would reduce that dependency's impact if it started failing. narration.text: Finish with the operational essentials for testing resilience. Chaos Engineering is hypothesis-driven: define expected behavior, introduce faults, and measure outcomes. AWS Fault Injection Simulator is a managed way to run repeatable experiments by declaring targets, actions, and stop conditions tied to CloudWatch metrics. Always scope experiments narrowly, define stop conditions that halt the run on unacceptable impact, and validate alerts and runbooks before widening scope. The most important habit is to iterate: run small experiments, learn, fix weakness, and automate the test so regressions are caught early. A reflection prompt: what small, safe experiment could you design today to validate a single resilience assumption in a system you manage?
